correctness.rationale: For p=36k+7, exponents 0,1,2,3,5 have no square factor 4 or 9; exponent 4 always has square factor 9. Every remaining square obstruction is q^2 for q>=5 with q<=sqrt(10^9). For each q and a, k lies in the single exact class (2^a-7)*36^{-1} modulo q^2 and is marked only after p-2^a>=q^2. Enumerating all k from 0 through floor((10^9-7)/36) therefore detects ALL simultaneous failures, not a bounded list of guessed candidates. Standalone verify.py checks that the complete obstructed-integer set is precisely nine values, checks primality of each via deterministic trial division up to sqrt(10^9), and factors p-64 for both qualifying primes. No speculative analytic extrapolation is used. The special p=7 has squarefree remainder p-1=6.

originality.rationale: The primary October 2026 paper classifies primes in exactly this residue class only below 10^8 and explicitly suggests finding the first with a_min>=6; its theorems on densities and unboundedness do not compute the first. Hercher gives a substantially wider representability computation for odd integers, but his reported table concerns a different unrestricted odd-integer first threshold and does not state the restricted-prime census or threshold. The finite first-exponent-six example and complete tenfold census are not literal or logical corollaries of those statements; the new exact sieve is needed. No equivalently formulated public prior result was found in targeted record and number searches. An unindexed computation or unreleased data could still cover this finite fact.

value.rationale: This is a motivated natural finite cutoff directly suggested in the conclusion of the source paper, rather than a random enumeration. It identifies the first occurrence of the new least-exponent layer a=6 in the precise prime progression under study, gives the entire layer through 10^9, and increases the published finite prime range tenfold. An exact modular-square obstruction enumeration eliminates infinitely many possible unknown factors by proving every possible q is covered. Its standalone certificate and nine-candidate reduction make the result reusable as a first threshold; no broader theorem is claimed or needed for value.
